entries.title: Remaining leads from the survey of comparable agent orchestrators (Oct 2026)
entries.body:
Leads borrowed from comparable open-source agent orchestrators, surveyed in October 2026 (first imported from issue #671).
Nothing here is a commitment; these are leads to triage.
The orch checked each against the code on 2026-11-17: ideas lym has built or that proved moot are dropped,
partly built ones name only what is still open, and the eight most worth doing are notes of their own in this project.
Each bullet names its source project and the lym module it would touch.

## Plan validation and concurrency (quarry, Plan-Write, board)

- **Typed scope operations on cards** (foremerge): each scope carries an additive or breaking operation,
  and deterministic rules flag colliding pairs even when files do not overlap.
  Worth comparing against board labels and the alignment gate.
- **Symbol leases between concurrent tasks** (Fusion, ORCH): expiring leases on symbol keys serialize overlapping tasks,
  with a deterministic tie-break; lym keeps overlapping tasks apart by board labels.
- **Commit-time reservation guard** (ntm): a pre-commit hook refuses a commit touching what another task holds; needs leases first.
- **Criterion amendment ledger** (oh-my-claudecode): a card's acceptance text changes only through a recorded amendment in weft.

## Review (burler, Bouncer)

- **Quorum of differently-angled judges** (ccswarm): lym fans out lenses but has no quorum vote for high-risk segments.
  Since 2026-11-19 a run's parent orch can be asked to see and veto each Code-Review round and each drift judge ruling
  (`code_review_ask_parent`, `judge_ask_parent`); that is one extra judge, not a quorum.
- **Risk tier by changed paths** (yylo): globs over sensitive paths choose the review depth and the gate scope.

## Engine, recipes and governance (shed, tender, orch, board)

- **Cross-run quarantine** (Bernstein): a task that fails three times across runs is held, unless the failures were the host's.
- **Fork a run from a step with a tree snapshot** (Bernstein): `shed goto` moves the cursor but does not restore the warp tree.
- **Warm retry guarded by a workspace hash** (Bernstein): resume the native session only when the tree is unchanged.
  Partly met since `dfade5f9a`: a run agent whose session a crash, reboot or killed pane ended resumes it (engines with a `SessionResumer`, so not Codex);
  no tree hash guards that resume, and a retry after a timeout or a finished run still starts fresh.
- **Evidence reuse by input identity** (yylo): verify is skipped on the same tree; a changed review prompt could rerun only the review.
- **Guidance at the next step boundary** (Conductor): a queue of operator guidance for the next producer's prompt.
  Partly met since 2026-11-19: `notify_parent_on` in `loom.yaml` mails the run's parent when a named row is reached,
  so the parent can brief that row's agent as it starts; there is still no queue of guidance lym itself folds into the prompt.
- **Batched operator questions with recorded assumptions** (Spec Kit `/clarify`, Conductor): Discussion-Write asks at most a few ranked questions,
  each with a recommended answer, and records unanswered ones as assumptions.
  Since 2026-11-19 a run's autonomous agents put their questions to the run's parent orch, not to the operator in their pane.
  Discussion asks in its pane only when `discussion_interactive` is `true`, which is off by default and forced off by autonomy mode (`30ed1ee58`),
  so this lead concerns an interactive Discussion only.
- **Rate-limit wait**: the orch watcher wakes the orch after a usage reset; tender itself schedules no resume.
- **Standing goals and scheduled routines** (ORCH, CAO, Fusion): periodic triage, dependency bumps or `selfreport` sweeps.

## Agent sessions (reed, shuttle)

- **Waiting-for-input signal** (agent-of-empires): shuttle has an awaiting-input state; screen heuristics still decide readiness and startup.
- **Reference status patterns and a paste pitfall** (CAO): compare its regexes and its tmux bracketed-paste note with shuttle's readiness and creel inject.
- **Context forecasting** (ntm): the orch cycles its context; Webster's Master and the loom driver do not, and nothing forecasts.
- **Staggered spawns** (ntm): space Webster forks and batten fan-out by learned rate limits.

## Observability (report, weft)

- **Hash-chained run journal** (Bernstein): a hash chain over producer outputs makes an archived run self-verifying.
- **Unverified-completion rate** (Bernstein): a `lym report` view of completions with no test or gate behind them.
- **Commit-to-record links** (AgentNote): weft links to warp by a `Warp-SHA:` trailer; a note or trailer on each warp commit could link back.
- **Run diff** (ccswarm): `lym report` comparing two archived runs' timelines and token use.
- **OpenTelemetry spans per producer** (Conductor).

## Operator attention (orch, dobby, reed)

- **Attention feed with acknowledgement states** (ntm): dobby's wait reminders have no seen, snoozed or acknowledged states.

## Discussion review (Discussion-Write, stencils, pattern)

- **Requirements-quality checklist** (Spec Kit `/checklist`): items with IDs the Discussion-review judge answers one by one.
- **Fixed analysis categories** (Kiro): inconsistency, ambiguity, conflicts, unstated assumptions and missing edge cases as named lenses.
- **PATTERN rules handed to reviewers** (Spec Kit constitution): its rules as numbered MUSTs in plan and code review prompts.
- **Glob-scoped steering** (Kiro): stencils pull per-area guidance chosen by the paths of a plan's glyphs.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Motif aim (operator, 2026-11-26)

Redesign this area around the ranking of `docs/research/platform/sandbox-without-new-kernel-2026-11-23.md` (`57d15cc02`): a seccomp connect supervisor over Landlock ABI 8 first, AppArmor per hub as the fallback, and decide what stays of the bwrap stages.
A closed area that refuses or hides the session bus must keep the strand pane memory cap (`10ae7e112`), which starts panes through the user manager.

## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The area matters most on the work machine OSL-1046 (operator, 2026-11-22).
On OSL-1046 sudo is tightly limited and does not cover AppArmor, so the profile `bwrap` needs on Ubuntu 24.04 cannot be loaded there; a `bwrap` area, and podman or Claude Code's `/sandbox`, which need the same user namespaces, are blocked on that machine until IT loads it.
Landlock needs no privilege, but the study `docs/research/platform/landlock-area-2026-11-23.md` (landed) found it does not close the two exposures below on kernel ABI 8 (Neve's measured; OSL-1046's by kernel version): a restricted child still reached the user bus and another hub's tmux socket, and `systemd-run --user` escapes the domain. On ABI 8 a Landlock area alone is a guardrail, not a barrier.
It recommends PreToolUse rows in `internal/shellguard` for the bus commands and other hubs' tmux servers, and re-running its probe on each new kernel.
The later study `docs/research/platform/sandbox-without-new-kernel-2026-11-23.md` (landed) finds that a seccomp filter handing every `connect()` to a supervisor in lym, stacked over Landlock ABI 8, closes both exposures with no root and no user namespace (measured on Neve; unmeasured on OSL-1046).
It recommends the shellguard rows now, that area when a barrier is wanted, after its probe has run on OSL-1046, and an AppArmor profile per hub as the fallback.
Of the shellguard rows, one is partly built: run sessions are refused raw `tmux` and `script`, the sampler excepted (`33cbce982`), which a script file or `eval` gets past; no row for the bus commands came with it.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/platform/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` was to stay writable for `branch.<b>.lymLocal`, but `fabric-remote-async` removed that mark and `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go`, so the reason is gone; whether git itself or another lym writer still needs `.git/config` writable is unchecked.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock alone controls no pathname socket until the kernel does (the Landlock study lists the five tasks that area takes; the later study puts Landlock ABI 8 under its seccomp supervisor instead), and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Cross-hub creel mail (`b30cccce2`): the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: Measure what Cortex XDR costs the test suites on OSL-1046
entries.brief: The 242 s fabricengine tier 1 against 37 to 41 s elsewhere is a machine difference no report has split
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-09)

Cortex XDR on OSL-1046 holds each new binary for about 10 s and scans each file a test creates, and fabricengine tests create many.
The shard report (`docs/research/speed/fabricengine-shards-2026-11-09/report.md`) put the 242 s one-process wall down to load, but the 2026-11-08 figure of 37 to 41 s was measured on another machine, so the gap is machine and Cortex, not load.
The package used 1.23 cores of 16 and `pmd` and `piud` were busy in nearly every sample.

## Idea

Separate the Cortex cost from the rest: the time a freshly built test binary waits before it runs, the time file creation takes with and without a scanned folder, and the fabricengine tier 1 wall with the repository and temp folders excluded from the scan, if the operator can have that changed.
The result says whether to cut tests, cut file and binary creation, or ask for an exclusion.

entries.title: Study whether the hardener finds and fixes real faults
entries.brief: Judge the two fabric hardener campaigns from their records: real findings, sound fixes, focus kept, cost
entries.body:
## Goal

Find out whether the hardener recipe does what it is for: drive the modules its focus names, find real faults, fix them with tests that hold, and converge.

## Evidence

- The first fabric campaign, `harden-fabricengine`, landed as `37649c772` after three rounds.
- The second, `harden-fabric-single-repo-verbs`, the one-repository fabric campaign with the fabric verbs in its sandbox, has landed as `2722a66ef`, so both campaigns are judged.
- The second campaign ran with the model rotation the template then set (opus, fable, sonnet).
  Hardener rounds now default to `sonnet[high]` alone, and a rotation is set per run through `hardener.reviewer` and `hardener.fixer` (`a66d41345`), so judge the rotation's cost and effect against that change.
- The five faults the second campaign found but could not raise were the task `harden-fabric-undriven-cases`, which has landed as `540e8c9b5`.
  Judge that fix as the campaign's follow-through.
- The cases round 3 left undriven (a discard or remove killed mid-operation, a fabric step that fails with no kill, and `adopt --archives`) were then driven by hand on a one-repository hub in the task `single-repo-undriven-cases`, landed as `dce6b8617` with the report `docs/research/single-repo-undriven-cases.md`.
  It found one fault the campaign's rounds had not: the killed run's `remove` record names `lym fabric remove <slug> --remote`, which answers `pair not found` once the pair is gone (the task `remove-record-rerun-pair-gone`).
  Judge it as a miss: could the campaign have reached it? The keep-local tag push was not among the cases it drove, and a real `adopt --archives` takeover needs a second machine, so the tags were pushed by hand.
- Each campaign's round files are under its records worktree at `_lym/reviews/harden/`: `round-<n>-focus.md`, `round-<n>-review.md`, `round-<n>-acceptance.md`, `round-<n>-usage.yaml` and the snapshots, beside its decision record and the landed commits.

## Questions

- **Findings**: for each finding, is it a real fault, a false positive or a matter of taste? Do its repro steps show it?
- **Fixes**: does each fix cure its finding? Does its regression test fail with the fix broken, as the fix rules demand? Was the package doc updated?
- **Focus**: did each round stay inside the campaign's focus? Did the focus files steer later rounds to what was left unverified?
- **Convergence**: did the Bouncer end the campaign on a sound verdict? Were deferred findings filed as open risks and on the board?
- **Misses**: which faults in the same code turned up after the campaign landed, outside it (such as the killed-seed way forward in `0e4782373`, the fetch prune in `f660ac101` and the remove record's way forward in `remove-record-rerun-pair-gone`), and could the campaign have reached them?
- **Cost**: tokens and wall time per round, from the usage files and the run's records.
- **Seen in the second campaign**: round 2's reviewer recorded smaller faults (O1 to O6) only as prose, since an incremental round admits only BLOCKING findings on changed hunks.
  Round 3's reviewer (sonnet, medium, 4 min) approved with half its focus undriven: the killed discard, the keep-local tag push, a failed step with no kill, and `adopt --archives` over real owner tags.
  A settled harden segment cannot be reopened (`lym loom goto` refuses), so the orch had no way to order another round. Judge each of these, and whether the remaining focus should block approval.
  Round 4 again raised what it found outside the incremental scope only as prose; those are the O1 to O5 that `harden-fabric-undriven-cases` fixed.
  A suspected cause is the stencils, not the model: `contracts/stencils/harden/harden-rubric-review.md` asks for OK, WARN or FAIL on every focus entry,
  while `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-review-format.md` lets an incremental round raise only BLOCKING findings on changed hunks, so such a round can only approve. Judge that conflict.
  Since `8cf7f4775`, a later hardener round cannot approve with its focus undriven:
  the reviewer raises a `decision`-class, BLOCKING, `origin: focus` finding for each focus entry it left undriven or marked WARN,
  `burlerengine.CheckReviewRound` exempts it from the changed-file rule, and the arbiter and then the parent rule on it.
  That answers whether the remaining focus should block approval going forward; judge the campaign's rounds as they ran, and whether the new finding is enough for the rubric conflict.

## Bounds

- Mostly a study of records and commits.
- At most three findings are reproduced, on a sandbox hub against the commit before their fix, one try each; no other trial runs.
- The report ends with a verdict and a short list of concrete changes to the hardener recipe or its stencils, each a candidate note.

entries.title: Keep the decision record and review findings of each landed task in the weft
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #229](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/229).

Import note: the issue names files under `.lym/`, which is deleted with its worktree, so only what the issue quotes of them reached the board: `_bolt/.lym/creel/journal`.

## Seen (operator, 2026-11-24)

An analysis of the parent's PR-Review findings in the C# hubs could not finish its work, because the evidence was gone.
About 29 findings were in scratchpad files under `/tmp` that no longer exist.
The decision records (Sketches) of the landed tasks could not be read: the board holds only open entries, and the task worktrees are deleted.
So the analysis could not say whether delivered code broke its decision record, and every gate attribution was inferred.
The only complete source left was each hub's creel mail journal under `_bolt/.lym/creel/journal`.

The operator wants this kept: absolutely.

## Idea

At landing, store what a later study needs in the weft, where it survives the worktree's deletion.

- The decision record with its `Added after Discussion` entries, as it stood at landing.
- Every Code-Review round's findings and the fixer reports, the parent's rulings and answers, and the PR-Review findings.
- The Describe text as it was merged, and the drift verdict.
- A short index row per landed task, so `lym report` can read them without walking directories.
- Read first which records survive today and where, and how landing already archives a run (the archive tag, `Reconcile leftover shuttle runs from run records`).
- Decide the weft path and how long records are kept, and make sure findings no longer live only in a scratchpad directory.

entries.title: Built-in run watch: mail the parent on every non-running state and on a gate slot held too long
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #222](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/222).

## What the orch does by hand today

In hub `dop`, the operator requires the orch to hear of every stop of every run it parents.
lym notifies some halts, but not all: a Webster block sends no notice (#207), and a gate whose testhost hangs past `timeout_min` holds its slot with no notice at all (#216).

So the orch keeps a Claude Code Monitor per run in flight: a shell loop that polls `lym loom status` in the task worktree every 30 s, prints on every change of state or producer, and prints a warning when `lym gate status` shows the run holding a gate slot past 45 minutes.
The Monitor expires after 30 minutes, so the orch re-arms it by hand, and a missed re-arm left a hung tier3 gate unseen for 21 hours.

## Wanted

lym itself watches every run in flight and mails its parent (creel) on:

- every state other than running: blocked, failed, paused, done, whatever the cause;
- a gate slot held by the run past a bound, such as 1.5 × the tier's `timeout_min`, naming the gate's PID and its child processes;
- optionally, every row change, for parents that want progress.

The watch lives in the dobby, not in the orch's session, so it needs no re-arming and survives the orch's context cycles.

entries.body:
Note `pr-ask-live-pane-test` is folded in only to be closed: it asks for a test of the parent-review ask this task removes.

Bundled from the notes below; each part keeps its note's text.

# Take the parent out of PR-Review; the earlier reviewers must catch what it finds

Imported from [issue #223](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/223).

## Seen (operator, 2026-11-24)

Today the parent orch can be asked to review at PR-Review, and the operator has used that a lot.
The operator now judges it a bad idea, for two reasons.

PR-Review is the very last gate, and it belongs to the human.
When a run reaches it, everything the LLMs and LoomYard can do should already be done.

A parent is also the wrong reviewer.
Asking the parent, which is the orchestrator, to review a Discussion or code is work for the orchestrator, and it costs more than a cold-start agent.
The reviewers a run already has should catch what the parent catches.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-26)

No agent reviews the pull request any more: when the PR is made, the agents are done.
What a parent finds when asked to review a PR must be found and fixed before the PR;
the checks that catch it are in the notes on reviewing the Describe text and on closing a task's scope at Code-Review.

## Idea

Take every agent out of PR-Review and add no seat in its place.

- Remove the parent's ask and re-ask from PR-Review in `internal/landingshed` and `internal/loomcli`.
- Remove PR-Review's own interactive session and its findings path: `pr_reviewer`, `lym loom pr-findings`, `pr_review_small_max`, `pr_review_ask_parent` and `pr_review_parent_timeout_min`.
- The row keeps only the mechanics the PR mode needs (see the note on the PR mode's three settings).
- Rely on the cold-start reviewers.
  The `review-code` fan already holds `code-scope`, which traces every decision of the record to a change in the diff and flags a decision no change builds, besides `code-correctness`, `code-affected-set` and `code-tests`.
  Read first which lenses the C# hubs run in `review-code` today, since the hub's own `lenses.yaml` and the C# layer can change the fan.
- Decide what a run does with a commit pushed to the PR branch by hand while it waits.


# A PR mode that registers the PR and approves it at once, with no agent under the block

Imported from [issue #224](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/224).

## Seen (operator, 2026-11-24)

The operator often wants a pull request registered on GitHub without looking at it.
With a beam, say P1, and several tasks under it, the operator wants each task to land as a PR that is approved at once and merged into the beam.
When all of P1 is done, one PR goes from P1 into its parent (P0 or root), and it lists every member PR.
That lets the operator backtrack and see how the work got where it is.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-26)

The PR block has three modes, and no LLM takes part in any of them:

- Manual: the PR is made and waits for the operator's own review and approval, as PR-Review is meant today.
- None: no PR; the row passes, as `pull_request` off does today.
- Trail (`pull_request: trail`, operator 2026-11-26): the PR is made and merged at once, with no agent and no human, so the beam's PR history can be backtracked.

How the three modes are configured is not decided yet.

## Idea

- Trail: the PR is made, no agent is spawned, and Finalize merges it at once, as it does today after the operator's `lym loom pr-continue`; merging a PR without an approval has long worked in lym.
- A beam's own PR lists its member PRs.
  `Rewrite a beam's pull request description after each member landing` (`1cd11ee5e`) may already do part of this; read what it writes before adding more.
- Manual waits for a human approval whatever the autonomy, which covers the note on autonomy and PR-Review.
- Read first where `beam.yaml` `pull_request` is read (`internal/landingshed`, `internal/pullrequest`) and how a run reaches Finalize today when a PR is approved.


# Autonomy: let PR review stay with the operator for one beam

Imported from [issue #217](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/217).

`beam.yaml: autonomy` is one switch for both halts and PR-Review requests. A hub wants the orch to settle halts on the prime autonomously while pull requests into the prime's branch (main) still wait for the operator's approval. Today that needs autonomy off, which also sends every halt to the operator, or autonomy on with the orch holding PR-Review by hand. Proposal: a separate key, such as `autonomy_pr_review: false`, so PR-Review requests on that beam or the prime go to the operator while halts stay autonomous.

## Issue comment, 2026-11-24

Seen again, with a merge into the prime's branch:

- The prime runs with `autonomy: true`, and the hub wants pull requests into main to wait for a human approval.
- The task `import-project-names` reached PR-Review; the parent answered the parent-review ask `--satisfied` and told the PR-Review agent by creel that landing waits on the operator's approval.
- `lym loom pr-continue` ran anyway about a minute later, and Finalize squash-merged the pull request into main once its gate passed, with no human approval on GitHub.

A message to the PR-Review agent is no way to hold a landing under autonomy: the satisfied answer alone ends the review.

Expected: a setting, per beam and for the prime, that keeps autonomy for halts but makes PR-Review wait for a human approval of the pull request (for example a GitHub approving review) before `pr-continue` or Finalize may merge.

# No tmux-tier test sends parent-review ask from a live non-orch pane

## Seen

`failed-ask-hides-satisfied` (issue 213) left out its item 3: no test runs `lym loom parent-review ask` from a live non-orch reed strand pane.
That is the path that failed twice on 2026-11-23 in the mo hub (creel refused the LOOM signature), and the fix (708cdadc5) is pinned only below the tmux tier.

## Idea

A tmux-tier test: a built lym binary in a reed strand pane, a hub with a pull request record under autonomy, and a live orch strand that receives the post; assert the ask is delivered and the parent's answer lets `pr-continue` end the review.

entries.title: Webster: plan fixes after begun batches, and recovery that ends asking
entries.body:
Bundled from the notes below; each part keeps its note's text.

# Plan fixes after begun batches block Webster; glyph-not-found on members a card creates

Imported from [issue #221](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/221).

## What happened

Two Webster halts after the plan was edited by a plan review/fix round while batches were already begun.

1. `blocked` / `escalation-to-human`:

```
webster: the auto-rebaseline of the changed plan blocks this run: webster: the edited plan changes the cards of a batch this run already begun: 00-overview.md changed outside its Card Index; it carries the plan's integration verify and only its Card Index is rebaselined; way forward: restore 00-overview.md, or fix the plan: move a done card's edit to a follow-up card after the last begun batch that carries the decision, with its Card Index line in 00-overview.md, then re-step the Webster row
```

2. After the plan was fixed and the run re-stepped, `failed` / `producer-hard-failure`, plan validation refused with four `glyph-not-found` findings, all of the form:

```
glyph-not-found/<card>[blocking]: target "<Unit>#<Member>"'s unit exists but the member is missing — check for a misspelled member
```

The members named were ones the plan's cards (5 and 6) introduce or modify, and the targets include a method signature with a generic parameter type (`IReadOnlyList<double>`) and a nullable (`TimeSpan?`).
Card 5 and card 6 cite the same new member as a target.

## Why abnormal

- The plan review loop (`Plan-Burler-Fix`) edited `00-overview.md` outside its Card Index and the run then blocked on it; the plan-fix stage gives no warning that such an edit is unrecoverable once a batch has begun, so each such fix costs an operator escalation.
- If the glyph targets name members that an earlier card of the same plan creates, validation cannot find them at plan time and refuses a valid plan. If they are misspelled, the finding text does not say which member of the unit is closest. Either way the finding should say whether the member is expected to be created by a card.
  I could not tell from the notes which case applies.

## What to do

- Have the plan-fix stage refuse or warn on edits to `00-overview.md` outside the Card Index once any batch has begun.
- Let glyph validation accept a target that an earlier card of the plan declares as created, and print the unit's actual member names beside a `glyph-not-found` finding.

Provenance: task `models-torque-drag-adapter`; notes `loom-halt-4.md`, `loom-halt-6.md`.


# Webster recovery ending dead with dead_reason asking drops the question and needs a manual reset

Imported from [issue #220](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/220).

## What happened

A Webster batch's verify failed on a test the plan could not satisfy.
The batch recovery session ended `dead` with `dead_reason: asking`, i.e. the recovery agent stopped to ask a question instead of finishing, and `recoveries: 1`, `recovery_retry: false`.
Then:

```
lym webster recover-batch 3 refused:
webster: batch 03-torque-drag-stage recovery (session ...) ended dead and the batch has no recovery left; way forward: end the run stuck, naming batch 03-torque-drag-stage
```

The run halted `blocked` (anomaly `escalation-to-human`).
After the plan was edited and rebaselined, Webster halted `blocked` again:

```
webster: a batch of this run is at a dead end: batch 03-torque-drag-stage is dead and its recovery earns no retry, so a Master would only end the run stuck on it; way forward: 1) lym webster reset --to batch-start --batch 03; 2) re-step the Webster row; or 1) lym webster reset --to start; 2) re-step the Webster row
```

## Why abnormal

A recovery agent that asks a question has no channel that answers it, so the question becomes a dead recovery with no retry.
The agent's question, which would tell the operator what is wrong, is not carried into the halt text: the halt note only restates "dead_reason: asking".
Plan edits made to fix the cause did not clear the dead state either; a manual `webster reset` was needed.

## What to do

- When a recovery ends with `dead_reason: asking`, put the agent's last message in the halt/refusal note.
- Either route the question to the parent (`lym creel post --parent --expect-reply`) or let a plan rebaseline that touches the dead batch's cards re-arm one recovery, so the operator does not need a reset.

Provenance: task `models-torque-drag-adapter`; notes `loom-halt.md`, `loom-halt-5.md`, `webster-refusal-recover-batch.md`.

entries.title: Gate test fixes for dotnet hubs: hung testhost, loggers, filters, tiers
entries.body:
Bundled from the notes below; each part keeps its note's text.

# Gate tier timeout_min does not stop a hung dotnet testhost; the slot stayed held 21 hours

Imported from [issue #216](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/216).

## What happened

In hub `dop`, run `models-torque-drag-adapter`, a Webster batch fork ran `lym gate test --tier tier3` at 2026-11-23 15:36.
Tier3 has `timeout_min: 35` in the gate config.
The tier's `dotnet test` testhost hung (about 4.5 min CPU in 21 h), and the gate slot stayed held for nearly 21 hours: `lym gate status` showed the slot held since 15:36 the next day.
The 35-minute bound never fired, so the fork, Webster and the run waited without any stop or notice to the parent orch.
Another hub's orch noticed the idle process; the parent orch killed the testhost by hand, and the gate then released its slot.

## Expected

At `timeout_min` the gate kills the tier's whole process tree (`sh -c dotnet test` → `dotnet` → `vstest` → testhost) and reports a timeout failure to its caller.

## Likely area

The timeout may kill only the direct child (`sh`), or wait on output pipes that the orphaned testhost still holds open, so the wait never returns.


## From issue #215

Imported from [issue #215](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/215).

On a Models hub, `lym gate test --wait --gate finalize` (PID 3536339) ran tier1, `dotnet test NORCE.Models.SlowTests -p:RunSlowTests=true` with `timeout_min: 30`, from 2026-11-23 15:36 to the next day, over 20 h. The test host had used about 7 min CPU; it was hung. The gate slot stayed held the whole time and the run sat at Finalize. On the same machine a DrillOpPlan hub's tier3 gate, started the same minute with a 35-minute bound, hung the same way and its bound never fired either. The machine may have been suspended overnight, but the bound did not fire before that either (15:36 + 30 min). Expected: the gate kills the tier's process tree at timeout_min and reports a timeout.

# gate test: reports 'ran no test' when the detailed console logger's summary is used

Imported from [issue #235](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/235).

With `--logger "console;verbosity=detailed"` passed to `lym gate test`, the gate reported that it ran no test, although the test log shows `Total tests: 1, Passed: 1`. The gate's test counter appears to misread the detailed logger's summary format.

This is abnormal because a passing run is reported as a run of nothing, which an agent may read as a failure or retry needlessly. The counter should parse the summary lines of every console logger verbosity, or read the result from a structured logger (trx) instead.

Provenance: task models-stick-slip-floor-tune, note Darn-Write.md.

# gate test: tier3 command already carries --filter, so a second --filter in args makes dotnet test refuse

Imported from [issue #234](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/234).

The tier3 command of `lym gate test` already carries a `--filter`. Passing a test filter in `{args}` adds a second `--filter`, and `dotnet test` refuses the call. An agent found that `-p:VSTestTestCaseFilter=...` works as an override, but nothing in the verb's help says so.

This is abnormal because selecting one test class is the common use of the verb. The gate should merge a caller filter into the tier's filter (or replace it) and document the way to do it.

Provenance: task models-stick-slip-floor-tune, note Darn-Write.md.

# gate test: darn-write gate key runs tier0 only, so a tier3 measurement test runs nothing

Imported from [issue #233](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/233).

A prompt told an agent to run a measurement test through `lym gate test --gate darn-write`. That gate key runs tier0 only, while the test lived in tier3 (a slow-test project, category `ModelsLong`). The first call ran no test, and the orch had to allow `--tier 3` by hand.

This is abnormal because the prompt and the gate key disagree on the tier. Either the prompt generator should pass `--tier` when the named test is not tier0, or the gate should say, when it runs no test, that the filter matches nothing at this tier and name the tiers that would match.

Provenance: task models-stick-slip-floor-tune, note Darn-Write.md.

# lym gate test answers that the hub declares no tier0, leaving a Burler fix round without a gate

Imported from [issue #237](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/237).

A Burler code fix round ran `lym gate test ./<module path>` on a Go module and the verb answered that the hub declares no tier0.
The round therefore had no gate, and the agent ran `go vet` and `go test` on the module directly.

This is abnormal because the fix-round instructions end each round with the gate; a hub without a declared tier0 leaves the round with nothing to run, and the agent improvised a substitute.

What to do: either have `lym gate test` fall back to a default tier when tier0 is undeclared, or make the refusal name the config key to add, and have the Burler code prompt say what to run when no gate exists.

Provenance: task slug timesheet-suggest-tool; notes burler-code-r1.md.

Bundled from the notes below; each part keeps its note's text.

# reed switch and a button's {strand} read the most recent client's session, not the clicker's

`switchClientVia` (`internal/reedengine/switch.go`) reads the clicking client's `#{session_id}` and `runButtonVia`'s strand lookup (`internal/reedengine/buttonclick.go`) reads `#{@lym_strand_name}`, each with `display-message -p -c <client>` and no `-t`.
Run from outside tmux, tmux expands that format against the most recently active client's session, so on a server with clients in several sessions `reed switch` can step from another client's session and a `{strand}` button can name another session's agent.
The RC click had the same defect and now reads its row of `list-clients -F`, which tmux expands per client; `TestClientAgentPane_ReadsEachClientsOwnSession` shows the two-client setup a test of these needs.

# Shellguard rows for the session bus

The study `docs/research/platform/sandbox-without-new-kernel-2026-11-23.md` (`57d15cc02`) ranks shellguard PreToolUse rows first:
refuse `systemd-run`, `busctl --user`, `dbus-send --session` and `gdbus` in run sessions, and `tmux -S` or `-L` aimed at another hub's server.
Raw `tmux` and `script` are already refused in run sessions (`33cbce982`); no row covers the bus commands.
Keep lym's own use of the bus, such as the strand pane's memory-capped scope (`10ae7e112`), working: the rows apply to agent commands only.

# creel post refusal after a persisted cd does not say why

Imported from [issue #245](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/245).

An agent's survey commands used `cd` into subdirectories, and the shell kept that directory for later calls.
The next `lym creel post` was refused because the working directory was no longer the anchored worktree root, which cost a retry.

Why it is abnormal:
- The shell's directory persisting across calls is easy to trip over, and the refusal surfaced only on the later creel call, away from the `cd` that caused it.

What to do:
- Have the refusal name the anchored root and say that a previous `cd` likely moved the shell, or accept calls from any directory inside the worktree.
- Mention in the agent guidance that `cd` persists and absolute paths or `git -C` avoid it.
